Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Cortex-dependent recovery of unassisted hindlimb locomotion after complete spinal cord injury in adult rats" for further consideration at eLife. Your revised article has been favorably evaluated by Eve Marder (Senior editor), a Reviewing editor, and three reviewers.

The manuscript has been improved but there are some remaining issues that need to be addressed before acceptance, as outlined below:

This revised study addresses most of the concerns raised by the reviewers. It has clarified issues regarding the biomechanical coupling and unassisted weight support which further helps to highlight the novelty of the study. The major strength of this report is in its focus on the circuits that are above the injury which may biomechanically influence the motor functions originally controlled by the injured cord. Although there is not a clear mechanistic explanation for the link between behavioral recovery, changes in cortical structures and the mechanical coupling the authors have gone a long way in the revision to explain how animals achieve training+treatment induced recovery and discussed the findings appropriately.

There remain some questions that the authors needs to respond to before the paper can be published:

1) There are significant concerns about the final figure showing the Western blots. Comments about this were made by reviewers in the previous round but it did not make it into the decision letter. First, several β actin control blots are reused across figures. I.e. in Figure B, the β actin control for PSD95 is the same as the control for synaptophysin. The authors should clarify that they were all taken from the same sheet. If they're not, then it's not appropriate to use the same β actin blot as a control for both cases. More confusing, however, are the blots in Figure C and D. The β actin controls appear to be the same for GLAST and ephrin A3, except that the final sample is missing in D. As for Figure B, if they were all on the same sheet, then this might be ok. But it appears to be more complicated. In C there are 5 samples for partial and 5 samples for complete; in D there are 4 samples for partial and 5 for complete. This explains why there's one less sample in the β actin control in D. However, this implies that there is a mismatch between columns in C and D, with the 5 complete animals matching up with different columns in the β actin controls (matching with 10-14 in C and with 9-13 in D). One can also see part of a blot clipped at the end of the ephrinA3 row. Please explain 1) whether the reused β actin controls were obtained from the sheet, 2) why there are 4 partial animals in some samples and 5 partials in others, 3) the apparent mismatch between columns in C and D, and 4) the apparently clipped blot in D.

Added by Senior Editor: it would be best if independent controls were used for each run. If they were run on one gel, then redesign the figure to make that clear and only show the control once if it was the same actual run used for multiple samples. fix this in some scientifically unassailable way or we won't be able to proceed to publication. Incorrectly replicated gel panels are one of the most common errors found in published papers, and we are starting to monitor papers for this kind of issue.

2) Please add the results from the bi-square vs. OLS regressions as a supplementary figure, along with your argument as to why the 'OLS' is preferred.

results.result: The authors challenge the prevailing assumption that the adult nervous system cannot develop extra-spinal recovery strategies to bypass spinal cord lesions. This assumption underlies both regeneration-based and bypass-based therapeutic approaches in the field.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, and C15 establish the background assumption being challenged. These are well-supported by general knowledge and citations to previous literature, accurately representing the field's understanding prior to this work.

results.result: Completely spinalized adult rats receiving combined pharmacological (5-HT agonists) and physical therapies (treadmill training and/or bike exercise) recovered unassisted hindlimb weight support and locomotion without spinal transmission through the lesion. Complete therapy was more effective than partial therapy, with animals achieving up to 56% weight-supported steps and significant improvements in open field scores by 12 weeks.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C21-C39, and C80 collectively demonstrate robust behavioral recovery with appropriate statistical analyses, multiple behavioral measures (treadmill %WSS and open field BBB scores), proper controls (sham therapy), and histological confirmation of complete lesions (C39). The correlation between treadmill and open field measures (C37, C38) strengthens the validity of the findings. Sample sizes appear adequate (n=15 per group) and statistical tests are appropriate.

results.result: Combined therapies induced therapy-dependent reorganization of the deafferented motor cortex, with significant expansion of trunk representation into the hindlimb cortex in animals receiving complete therapy. This expansion correlated with motor performance and was not due to increased cortical excitability.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C48 demonstrate cortical motor reorganization with appropriate statistical analyses (2-way ANOVA), proper controls (naïve intact animals, threshold current measurements), and correlations with behavioral outcomes. The absence of hindlimb representations (C40) confirms lesion completeness. The specific expansion of trunk but not forelimb or vibrissae representations (C45, C46) supports the specificity of the reorganization.

results.result: Lesioning the reorganized motor cortex reversed hindlimb motor recovery without affecting forelimb function, demonstrating that cortical reorganization is causally responsible for the observed behavioral recovery. The same lesion in naïve intact animals produced no functional impairment.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C49-C58, and C91 provide strong causal evidence through cortical lesion experiments with appropriate controls (naïve intact animals, C57) and specificity (preserved forelimb function, C53-C56). The video analysis (C50, C51, C111) identifies plantar contact as the key differentiating feature. Statistical analyses are appropriate (2-way ANOVA). This is a critical experiment establishing causality rather than mere correlation.

results.result: Combined therapies promoted sprouting of corticospinal axons from the deafferented hindlimb cortex into the gray matter of the thoracic spinal cord above the lesion. Animals receiving complete therapy showed significantly more axonal sprouting than sham therapy animals or naïve intact controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C7, C59-C63 demonstrate anatomical plasticity with appropriate methods (anterograde tracing with BDA), proper controls (naïve intact and sham therapy), and statistical analyses (2-way ANOVA). However, the sample size is very small (n=2 per group), which is a significant limitation. The rostro-caudal gradient (C59) and increased sprouting with therapy (C60-C62) are consistent with the functional findings, but the mechanistic link to trunk control (C63) remains inferential.

results.result: Combined therapies induced expansion of forepaw somatosensory representation into the deafferented hindlimb cortex, with spatial overlap between the expanded trunk motor and forepaw sensory representations. This integrated sensorimotor reorganization likely contributes to motor recovery.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C18, C64-C74 demonstrate somatosensory reorganization with chronic recordings, appropriate statistical analyses (GZLM for binary data), and spatial mapping. The overlap with motor reorganization (C70) is compelling. The observation that hindlimb cortex neurons respond to forepaw placement during normal locomotion (C72-C74) provides a substrate for reorganization. However, the causal contribution to recovery (C71) remains inferential as sensory and motor contributions were not disentangled.

results.result: Adult rats developed a novel cortical sensorimotor circuit that bypasses the spinal lesion through biomechanical coupling, integrating forepaw sensory input with trunk motor control to enable hindlimb weight support via activation of trunk muscles spanning the lesion.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C20, C82, C83, C100, and C108 propose a biomechanical coupling mechanism, but this remains speculative (explicitly noted as 'probably' in C9, C20, C108). While the anatomical substrate exists (trunk muscles spanning the lesion, C82) and the sensorimotor reorganization is demonstrated, direct evidence of biomechanical coupling is lacking. The mechanism is inferred from the pattern of reorganization and behavioral outcomes but not directly tested. Additional experiments measuring trunk muscle activity, biomechanical forces, or testing predictions of the biomechanical coupling hypothesis would be needed to fully support this claim.

results.result: Previous studies achieved hindlimb locomotion recovery in adult spinalized rats but required external support or stimulation. Recovery without such support was believed restricted to neonatally spinalized rats due to higher plasticity. This study demonstrates that combined therapies can produce sufficient cortical plasticity in adult rats to achieve unassisted recovery.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C79 and C84-C88 accurately represent prior work through appropriate citations and correctly position the current findings as advancing beyond previous limitations. The comparison to neonatal spinal injury models (C84-C87) provides important context. Claim C88 is well-supported by the experimental data showing recovery in adult animals.

results.result: The complete thoracic transection model excludes any spinal transmission of motor commands through the lesion, confirmed by both physiological evidence (no movement elicited below the lesion by cortical microstimulation) and anatomical evidence (histological verification with Nissl and 5-HT staining).
results.evaluation: Claims C16, C81, and C39 establish the completeness of the spinal lesion through multiple lines of evidence. The motor mapping showing no hindlimb responses (C81, also C40) and histological confirmation in all animals (C39) provide strong support. This is critical for the interpretation that recovery occurs without spinal transmission through the lesion.

results.result: The overlap of sensorimotor reorganization unifies previous separate findings on motor and sensory plasticity, represents genuinely cortical plasticity, and is likely a key factor for functional recovery. The motor cortex is required to sustain recovered locomotion after complete spinal cord injury.
results.evaluation: Claims C89, C90, C95, and C99 synthesize the findings and place them in context of prior literature. The integration of motor and sensory reorganization (C89, C90) is well-supported by the data. The requirement of motor cortex for recovered locomotion (C95) is strongly supported by the lesion experiments. The claim of genuinely cortical plasticity (C99) is supported by the cortical mapping and lesion data, though subcortical contributions cannot be excluded (acknowledged in C98).

results.result: The cortical lesion produced no functional impairment in naïve intact animals, consistent with prior findings that motor cortex is required for learning but not executing learned motor skills in normal rats. The similarity to neonatal spinal injury suggests combined therapies may rescue critical period plasticity features.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C94 are supported by control experiments (C57) and appropriate citations. Claim C96 is a reasonable inference from the similarity between adult and neonatal recovery patterns, supported by citations, though it remains somewhat speculative about the underlying mechanisms.

results.result: Spinal cord injury leads to dramatic loss of motor function and often permanently compromises locomotion. Recovery approaches include healing the lesion to re-establish pathways or bypassing the lesion to reconnect circuits, both addressing the limited regenerative capacity of the adult spinal cord.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C14 accurately represent established knowledge in the field, supported by appropriate citations. These provide necessary background context for the study.

results.result: Therapeutic interventions can act at multiple levels of the sensorimotor system and may have redundant or synergistic effects. Well-designed combinations of therapies should be employed to maximize corticospinal plasticity and functional outcomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C17, C103-C105 are supported by appropriate citations and are consistent with the study's findings showing superior outcomes with combined therapies. The recommendation for combination therapies (C105) is a reasonable inference from the current results.

results.result: The observed corticospinal sprouting is consistent with many previous studies in various spinal cord injury models. While subcortical plasticity likely contributed to recovery, at least part of the plasticity is genuinely cortical.
results.evaluation: Claims C97 and C98 appropriately contextualize the findings within prior literature and acknowledge the likely contribution of subcortical plasticity while arguing for genuine cortical plasticity based on the cortical mapping and lesion data.

results.result: Patients recovering from spinal cord injury use upper limbs with walking aids, switching from bipedal to quasi-quadrupedal locomotion. Supraspinal control of trunk stability might become critical for locomotion in recovering patients, as observed in the experimental animals.
results.evaluation: Claims C101 and C102 attempt to translate the quadrupedal rat findings to bipedal human locomotion. While C101 is supported by citation, C102 is highly speculative. The translational relevance of trunk control in quadrupedal rats to bipedal human locomotion with assistive devices remains uncertain and would require clinical validation.

results.result: This study raises the standard for behavioral recovery achievable without spinal transmission through the lesion. Future work attempting to restore spinal communication should consider that recovery may be unrelated to restored spinal communication. Therapies should leverage plasticity along the entire neural axis.
results.evaluation: Claims C106, C107, and C109 are reasonable inferences and recommendations based on the study's findings. They appropriately highlight the implications for interpreting recovery mechanisms in future studies and for therapeutic development.

results.result: The study used 74 adult female Sprague-Dawley rats divided across three experiments examining behavioral recovery with cortical mapping and lesioning, tract tracing, and somatosensory mapping.
results.evaluation: Claim C110 accurately describes the experimental subjects and design. The sample sizes appear adequate for the behavioral and mapping experiments, though the tract tracing experiment has very small sample sizes (n=2 per group).

results.result: The percentage of plantar steps was markedly higher in animals with good recovery (performers) and significantly decreased after cortical lesion in performers but not in animals with poor recovery (non-performers).
results.evaluation: Claim C111 is supported by video analysis with appropriate statistics. This provides additional detail on the mechanism by which cortical lesions reverse recovery, identifying plantar stepping as the key affected feature.
